ta-l3d24q1-d1e105.summary: Divisio textus and plan for Distinction 24. Having treated faith in its substance (d. 23), Lombard now treats it in relation to its object, prompted by the Apostle's description of faith as the 'argument of things not appearing'. The section has two parts: whether faith concerns what is not seen, and whether it concerns what is unknown. In the first, Lombard shows that faith properly concerns the unseen and answers the objection about whether Peter had faith in the passion he witnessed. The question has three articles: what the object of faith is, how it relates to our knowledge, and the merit and praise of faith.
claims: Distinction 24 treats faith in relation to its object, after Distinction 23 treated it in itself.
Faith properly concerns what is not seen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e131.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is uncreated truth the object of faith?): faith concerns what the creed contains, and the creed contains things about creatures, such as the passion. So faith's object is not only uncreated truth.
claims: The creed's created content shows that faith's object is not solely uncreated truth.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e134.summary: Second objection: faith is instructed by Scripture, which contains much about creatures.
claims: Scripture's teaching about creatures extends faith's object beyond uncreated truth.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e137.summary: Third objection: faith began from prophetic revelation, which concerns created things subject to time. So faith does too.
claims: Faith, originating in prophecy about temporal things, concerns created realities.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e140.summary: Fourth objection: a universal form does not move to action, being removed from motion (De anima III). First truth is even more removed from matter and motion. Since faith is in a way operative, working through love (Galatians 5:6), its object cannot be first truth.
claims: As universal forms do not move to action, first truth cannot be the object of an operative habit.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e144.summary: Fifth objection: the theological virtues order us to the end, and our end is not only God but also created glory. So faith concerns created truth as well.
claims: Since created beatitude is part of our end, faith concerns created truth.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e147.summary: Sed contra: Dionysius says divine faith concerns the simple and ever-existing truth, which is uncreated truth.
claims: Faith concerns simple, eternal, uncreated truth.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e150.summary: Second sed contra: a thing is named from what gives it species, and habits take their species from their object. Since faith is called theological from God, its proper object is uncreated truth.
claims: Faith's name as a theological virtue shows that its object is uncreated truth.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e159.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (does faith concern complex truth, i.e. propositions?): faith's object is simple truth, in which there is no complexity.
claims: The simplicity of faith's object excludes propositional complexity.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e162.summary: Second objection: vision succeeds faith, and the vision of the homeland will be of something incomplex. So faith is too.
claims: Faith's successor, beatific vision, is of the incomplex, so faith is as well.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e165.summary: Third objection: faith is formed by charity, whose object is incomplex good. So faith's object is incomplex truth.
claims: Charity's incomplex object suggests an incomplex object for faith.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e168.summary: Fourth objection: time enters the composition of concepts (De anima III), but time does not seem to belong to the substance of faith; otherwise at Christ's birth only those who believed he was being born then would have been faithful.
claims: Since time is not essential to faith, its object is not tensed propositions.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e172.summary: Fifth objection: faith is always the same, but propositions change: we believe Christ born, the fathers believed him to be born. So faith is not of propositions.
claims: Faith's sameness across time is incompatible with changing propositions.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e175.summary: Sed contra: faith is between opinion and science, both of which concern propositions.
claims: Like science and opinion, faith concerns propositions.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e178.summary: Second sed contra: the believer differs from the unbeliever by faith, not by an incomplex object: Jews believe in Christ's coming as we do, but we believe he has come while they await his coming. So faith concerns complexes.
claims: Believers and unbelievers differ over propositions, not incomplex objects.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e187.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (can faith be subject to falsehood?): every contingent truth can be false, and faith includes contingent truths, such as the passion, which depended on the free will of Christ and of his persecutors.
claims: Contingent truths under faith could be false, so faith can be false.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e190.summary: Second objection: after Abraham believed in the future passion, God could still have redeemed humanity another way, and then Abraham's faith would have been falsified.
claims: God's power to redeem otherwise makes Abraham's faith potentially false.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e193.summary: Third objection: hope can be false, since one may hope for eternal life and never attain it; so can charity, as when one promises out of charity what one does not do (Paul in 1 Corinthians). So faith can too.
claims: Since hope and charity can be deceived, faith can be.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e196.summary: Fourth objection: latria is directed by faith, yet one can err in latria, as by adoring an unconsecrated host thought consecrated. So faith can be subject to falsehood.
claims: Errors in worship directed by faith show faith can be false.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e200.summary: Sed contra: faith is more certain than science, and science is not subject to falsehood.
claims: Faith, more certain than science, cannot be false.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e203.summary: Second sed contra: no virtue produces a bad act, and believing falsehood is a bad use of the intellect. Since faith is a virtue, nothing false falls under it.
claims: As a virtue, faith cannot produce false belief.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e213.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1. In the object of a power three things can be considered: the formal (as light in the object of sight, making colour actually visible), the material (colour itself, potentially visible), and the accidental (quantity and the like accompanying colour). Since the object acts on a passive power through its form, powers and habits are specified by the formal ratio of their object. In faith, nothing is actually credible except through first truth, since faith assents only on account of first truth, as colour is visible only through light. So first truth is the formal element in the object of faith, from which the whole ratio of the object derives. Whatever is believed about God, such as that he suffered, is material, and what follows from these credibles is accidental. Properly speaking, the object of faith is first truth.
claims: The object of a power has formal, material and accidental elements, and the formal ratio specifies the power.
First truth is the formal object of faith, as light is of sight.
What is believed about God, such as the passion, is the material object of faith; what follows from it is accidental.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e216.summary: Reply to the first objection: the passion and other created matters in the creed stand materially to the object of faith.
claims: Created articles are the material object of faith.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e219.summary: Reply to the second objection: Scripture instructs faith both in its essentials (what it says about God) and in accidentals (the deeds of the fathers and the like), which pertain to faith insofar as they are divinely inspired and spoken.
claims: Scriptural narratives pertain to faith accidentally, as divinely inspired.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e222.summary: Reply to the third objection: faith and prophecy concern the same thing, like the passion, but under different aspects. Faith regards formally the eternal element (that God suffered) and materially the temporal; prophecy the reverse.
claims: Faith and prophecy concern the same events, faith formally regarding the eternal and prophecy the temporal.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e226.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: universal forms move not as universal but as applied to something particular; likewise first truth moves to action as applied to this or that, as when considered as the end one can reach. Alternatively, universal forms do not subsist and so cannot be principle or term of action, which is not true of God, who subsists in himself.
claims: First truth moves to action as applied to a particular agent's end.
Unlike non-subsistent universals, God subsists and can be principle and term of action.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e229.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: created beatitude consists in our operation directed to God, and operations are known through their objects. So faith concerns God principally and created beatitude secondarily.
claims: Faith concerns God principally and created beatitude secondarily.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e238.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: believing is thinking with assent, and one can assent only to what is true, and truth exists only in composition of concepts or words. So the object of faith must be complex truth, which is why some philosophers called the composing and dividing operation 'faith'. Those who said faith's object is incomplex misused the term: 'I believe the incarnation' cannot mean forming the concept of the incarnation (then anyone who understood the word would believe), but 'I believe that the incarnation is or was'. This also follows from faith's proper object, first truth, of which we cannot know what it is so as to grasp it by simple apprehension, but only that it is, which is known by composing and dividing.
claims: Since assent is to truth and truth is in composition, faith's object is a complex truth.
'I believe the incarnation' means 'I believe that the incarnation is or was'.
Because we cannot know what first truth is, our knowledge of it is propositional.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e241.summary: Reply to the first objection: first truth is simple in reality but contains many aspects according to reason, as the intellect forms diverse concepts of it, and it can compose and divide these and form propositions about God.
claims: The intellect forms many concepts of the simple God and composes them into propositions.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e244.summary: Reply to the second objection: composing and dividing resolve into the operation that regards the incomplex, since what a thing is is the principle of knowing whether and that it is. So what succeeds faith and consummates it will be vision of the incomplex.
claims: Propositional knowledge resolves into knowledge of the incomplex, which beatific vision provides.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e247.summary: Reply to the third objection: charity's object is the good, which is in things, but faith's object is the true, which is completed in the soul's operation. Since composition and division exist only in the soul, the complex is faith's object even though the incomplex is charity's.
claims: Good is in things and truth is in the mind, so charity's object is incomplex and faith's complex.
concepts: bonum in rebus, verum in mente

ta-l3d24q1-d1e251.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: determinate time is accidental to faith, as it is to the predicate and subject the intellect composes. What is accidental to faith is not necessary for salvation until determined by preaching and teaching.
claims: The time of an article is accidental to faith and becomes necessary only when determined by teaching.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e254.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: some who held faith to be of propositions said the same proposition varies across three tenses, which was rejected in Book I, d. 24. Others said the articles are the same not in essence but in utility, which is also wrong, since faith would then be the same only secundum quid. Rather, in an article there is something material (the passion), something formal (the divine reality) and something accidental (the time). So faith varies not in essence but only in accident.
claims: The tensed variation of articles concerns only their accidental element, time, so faith remains essentially the same across history.
concepts: material, formal, accidental in an article

ta-l3d24q1-d1e263.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: faith rests on first truth, which is infallible, so nothing false can fall under faith.
claims: Because faith rests on infallible first truth, nothing false can fall under it.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e266.summary: Reply to the first objection: the contingent is an object of faith only as it falls under divine foreknowledge, where it has necessity of consequence. As foreknowledge cannot be deceived, neither can faith.
claims: Contingent events fall under faith as foreknown by God, with necessity of consequence.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e269.summary: Reply to the second objection: by absolute power God could have redeemed humanity otherwise after Abraham's time, but not as considered in relation to his foreknowledge, since what God foreknows cannot fail to happen. Abraham's faith concerned the passion as it falls under divine foreknowledge.
claims: God's absolute power to redeem otherwise does not falsify faith, which concerns events as foreknown.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e272.summary: Reply to the third objection: hope tends to beatitude only on the supposition of merits, otherwise it would be presumption, so hope is not deceived if merits fail. Nor is charity deceived, since it always wills what pleases God; if one later finds that something did not please God, it is human estimation that erred, not charity.
claims: Hope is conditional on merit and charity wills what pleases God, so neither is deceived; only human estimation errs.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e276.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: faith concerns only a duly consecrated host; that this host is duly consecrated is a matter of human estimation, which is where error in latria can arise.
claims: Faith concerns the consecrated host as such; whether a particular host is consecrated is human judgment.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e294.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (can faith be of things seen?): 'we see now through a mirror in an enigma' (1 Corinthians 13:12) refers to faith, so faith is a vision and what is believed is seen.
claims: Paul calls faith a kind of seeing.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e300.summary: Second objection: the light of faith stands to the articles as natural light to naturally known principles, and natural light makes self-evident principles seen. So the light of faith makes the articles seen.
claims: By analogy with natural light, the light of faith makes the articles seen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e303.summary: Third objection: to understand is to see, and the hearer must understand what is said in order to believe. So faith, which comes from hearing, is of things seen.
claims: Belief requires understanding, which is a kind of seeing.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e306.summary: Fourth objection: prophecy causes vision, and faith and prophecy concern the same things.
claims: Faith, sharing prophecy's objects, concerns things seen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e310.summary: Fifth objection: the material object of faith is created, and such things, like the passion, can be seen even by the senses. Since faith concerns its whole object, it concerns things seen.
claims: Faith's material object can be sensibly seen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e313.summary: Sed contra: faith is the argument of things not appearing (Hebrews 11:1).
claims: Faith concerns things not appearing.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e324.summary: Second sed contra: no one has ever seen God (John 1:18), and faith properly concerns God.
claims: Since God is unseen, faith concerns the unseen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e335.summary: Third sed contra: faith begets hope (a gloss on Matthew 1), and hope concerns what is unseen (Romans 8).
claims: Faith, the source of hope, also concerns the unseen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e347.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (can faith be of things known scientifically?): that God exists is believed, yet it is known, having been demonstrated.
claims: God's existence is both believed and demonstrated.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e350.summary: Second objection: teaching is one source of science, and faith comes by teaching as to the distinction of what is to be believed (Romans 10). So faith is of things known.
claims: Faith comes through teaching, which produces science.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e353.summary: Third objection: whatever has a probative reason is known, and matters of faith have such reasons: 1 Peter 3:15 bids us give a reason for our faith, the Commentator on Dionysius says reason is prior to authority, and Richard of St Victor says reason is never lacking to prove any truth.
claims: Matters of faith can be proven by reason and are thus known.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e359.summary: Fourth objection: every proof compelling assent produces science, and miracles compel assent to matters of faith, as with the demons.
claims: Miracles compel assent and so produce science of what is believed.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e363.summary: Sed contra: science is caused by understanding of principles, which we cannot have of matters of faith while faith remains, in this life.
claims: Without understanding of their principles, matters of faith cannot be known scientifically.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e366.summary: Second sed contra: science is an effect of reason, and matters of faith are above reason.
claims: What is above reason cannot be known by science.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e369.summary: Third sed contra: no one has ever seen God (John 1:18), and faith properly concerns God.
claims: Faith concerns the unseen God.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e386.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (are the things of faith unknown?): Gregory says apparent things are not objects of faith but of acknowledgement; what lacks acknowledgement is unknown. So objects of faith are unknown.
claims: Objects of faith lack agnitio and so are unknown.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e389.summary: Second objection: 'eye has not seen nor ear heard, nor has it entered the human heart' (1 Corinthians 2:9). Whatever is known enters the heart, so faith concerns the unknown.
claims: What has not entered the heart is unknown, and faith concerns such things.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e400.summary: Third objection: all our knowledge originates in sense, and the objects of faith cannot be reduced to sensible knowledge. So there is no knowledge of them.
claims: Objects of faith, irreducible to sense, cannot be known.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e403.summary: Fourth objection: whatever is known is somehow present to the knower, but faith concerns absent things (Augustine).
claims: Faith concerns the absent, which cannot be known.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e407.summary: Sed contra: every habit in a cognitive power makes its object known, and faith is in a cognitive power as subject (d. 23, q. 2, a. 3).
claims: Faith, a cognitive habit, makes its objects known in some way.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e410.summary: Second sed contra: unbelief is ignorance (1 Timothy 1:13), so faith is knowledge and what is believed is known.
claims: As unbelief is ignorance, faith is knowledge.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e428.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1. Vision properly is the act of sight, and because of sight's nobility the name is transferred to other cognitive powers by likeness. If the likeness is only in the genus of knowledge, every knowing is loosely called seeing, and in that sense faith is of things seen by an inner, not outer, sight, as Lombard says. If the likeness extends to the mode of knowing, seeing occurs when an intelligible form is actually formed in the intellect by intellectual light, natural (as in grasping a quiddity) or supernatural (as in the vision of God in the homeland). By extension, propositions known from such vision are seen, as first principles by natural light or prophetic visions by supernatural light, and so are conclusions resolved into these principles by demonstration. In this proper sense faith cannot concern things seen, since its principal object, God, escapes the formation of our intellect in this life and is not accessible to it (Augustine), and we cannot reduce the matters of faith to seen principles by demonstration.
claims: 'Vision' applies loosely to all knowledge and properly to knowledge in which the intelligible form is present by intellectual light.
Properly seen are quiddities, first principles, prophetic content, and demonstrated conclusions.
Faith is not of things seen in the proper sense, because God escapes our intellect's formation in this life and the articles cannot be demonstrated.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e431.summary: Reply to the first objection: 'vision' there is taken broadly, in the first sense.
claims: Paul's 'seeing in a mirror' uses vision in the broad sense.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e434.summary: Reply to the second objection: the terms of naturally known principles are comprehensible to our intellect, so knowledge of those principles is vision. Not so with the terms of the articles. In the future, when God is seen by essence, the articles will be self-evident and seen as principles of demonstration are now.
claims: The terms of the articles are not comprehensible to us now, so the light of faith does not make them seen.
In the beatific vision the articles will be self-evident like first principles.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e437.summary: Reply to the third objection: what precedes belief is understanding what the name signifies, not what the thing is, since names are imposed from effects.
claims: Belief requires understanding the meaning of the words, not the essence of the thing.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e441.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: prophecy regards the temporal as its proper object, which the intellect can comprehend, so prophecy is vision.
claims: Prophecy is vision because its proper object, the temporal, is comprehensible.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e444.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: faith concerns its material object, such as the incarnation, only as it falls under the formal object, as sight concerns colour only as lit. In that respect it falls under neither bodily nor intellectual sight.
claims: Faith attains its material object only under its formal ratio, which is unseen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e453.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: things pertain to faith either per se or per accidens. What is per se to faith belongs to it always and everywhere, while what belongs to faith only on account of this or that person is accidental. What wholly exceeds human intellect, concerns God, and is divinely revealed belongs to faith per se. What exceeds the intellect only of some people belongs to faith per accidens. What exceeds all human intellect cannot be demonstrated, since demonstration rests on understanding of principles, so it cannot be known scientifically. But the preambles to faith, such as that God exists, can be demonstrated and known, and are believed only by those whose intellect does not reach the demonstration. For faith of itself inclines sufficiently to all that accompanies, follows or precedes it.
claims: What exceeds all human understanding belongs to faith per se and cannot be known scientifically.
Preambles such as God's existence can be demonstrated and are believed only per accidens by those who cannot follow the demonstration.
Faith inclines sufficiently to everything that accompanies, follows or precedes it.
concepts: per se and per accidens objects of faith

ta-l3d24q1-d1e456.summary: Reply to the first objection: the solution is clear from what was said.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e459.summary: Reply to the second objection: faith is determined by hearing a teaching that proposes what to avoid and what to hold but does not prove it. Such teaching does not produce science.
claims: Teaching that proposes without proving does not produce science.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e462.summary: Reply to the third objection: human reason precedes human authority, and divine reason precedes divine authority, on which faith rests. Our faith stands to the divine reason by which God knows as one who assumes the principles of a subalternate science stands to the subalternating science that proves them. So the Apostle does not urge human reason to prove the faith, but the divine reason, showing that God has spoken. Human reason is to defend the faith, showing that its presuppositions are not impossible, not to prove the articles sufficiently. Richard's dictum concerns not sufficient proof but persuasive arguments.
claims: Faith stands to God's knowledge as a subalternate science to its subalternating science.
Human reason defends faith by showing its claims are not impossible, but cannot prove the articles.
The reason Christians give for their faith is the divine reason, the evidence that God has spoken.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e466.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: arguments that compel faith, like miracles, do not prove the articles themselves but the truthfulness of the one who announces the faith, so they do not produce science of what is believed.
claims: Miracles prove the credibility of the messenger, not the content of the faith.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e475.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: perfect intellectual knowledge requires three things: that the object be proposed to the intellect, that the intellect adhere to it, and that it see it. Matters of faith are proposed not in themselves but in words insufficient to express them and in likenesses that fall short of representing them, which is why they are known 'in a mirror and an enigma'. So they are not properly seen, but the intellect assents to them. They are therefore known imperfectly, and not wholly unknown.
claims: Perfect knowledge requires proposal, adherence and vision.
Matters of faith are proposed in inadequate words and likenesses and adhered to without being seen.
Objects of faith are known imperfectly, neither seen nor wholly unknown.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e478.summary: Reply to the first objection: Gregory speaks of perfect acknowledgement, which includes vision.
claims: Gregory's agnitio means perfect knowledge including vision.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e481.summary: Reply to the second objection: what 'enters the heart' is what can be formed by the heart's operation, that is, what is seen. In that sense what God has prepared does not enter the human heart.
claims: Divine gifts do not enter the heart in the sense of being seen.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e484.summary: Reply to the third objection: the knowledge of faith originates in sense insofar as it knows the meanings of words presented to the senses, but these fall short of representing what faith is properly about. So faith lacks perfect knowledge.
claims: Faith's knowledge begins from sensibly presented words but they do not adequately represent its object.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e488.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: properly present is that whose essence is presented to intellect or sense, which produces vision. So Augustine says present things are seen and absent things believed, and faith is likened to hearing, since by hearing we know absent things recounted to us.
claims: Things are present when their essence is presented, which yields vision; faith, being of the absent, resembles hearing.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e506.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 1 (is it necessary to believe what one neither knows nor sees?): providence perfectly provides for a thing when it gives it the means to reach its end, and providence provided sufficiently for human nature at creation. So natural reason suffices to order humans to their end, and no belief above reason is needed.
claims: Providence equipped human nature to reach its end by natural reason.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e509.summary: Second objection: our last end is God as the highest good, and natural reason proves that there is a highest good. So nothing beyond natural reason need be believed.
claims: Natural reason knows the highest good, which suffices for the end.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e512.summary: Third objection: divine wisdom infinitely exceeds our reason, so infinitely many things in it exceed reason, and we cannot know them all. By parity, we need know none of the things above reason.
claims: Since we cannot know all that exceeds reason, we need know none of it.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e515.summary: Sed contra: a higher life requires a higher operation, and the life of grace is higher than that of nature. So the knowledge of grace must exceed that of nature.
claims: The higher life of grace requires knowledge beyond nature.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e519.summary: Second sed contra: faith is the substance of things hoped for, and what we hope for is above reason (1 Corinthians 2:9). So faith must concern what is above reason.
claims: Faith, concerning what is hoped for, must reach above reason.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e539.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 2 (is believing the unseen praiseworthy and meritorious?): one who believes quickly is light of heart (Sirach 19:4), and one who believes what they in no way see believes too quickly.
claims: Believing the wholly unseen is credulity.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e545.summary: Second objection: renouncing reason, our noblest part, is blameworthy, and one who believes what is not consonant with reason renounces it.
claims: Belief beyond reason renounces reason and so is blameworthy.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e548.summary: Third objection: discernment makes every human work praiseworthy, and all our discernment is by reason. In what is beyond reason we have nothing to discern with, so one could believe falsehood as easily as truth.
claims: Without rational discernment, belief beyond reason is indiscriminate.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e551.summary: Sed contra: 'blessed are those who have not seen and have believed' (John 20:29).
claims: Believing without seeing is blessed.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e563.summary: Second sed contra: every act of virtue is in itself meritorious and praiseworthy, and believing the unseen is the act of faith, a virtue.
claims: As a virtuous act, believing the unseen is meritorious.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e572.summary: First objection to quaestiuncula 3 (does human reason diminish the merit of faith?): a sufficiently probative reason would wholly remove faith's merit, since 'faith has no merit where human reason provides proof' (Gregory). So a somewhat persuasive reason diminishes it.
claims: If full proof removes merit, partial persuasion diminishes it.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e578.summary: Second objection: what leads to the corruption of faith diminishes its merit, and arguments and disputations corrupt faith (Averroes): hearing other views makes one adhere less to what one is used to and begin to doubt.
claims: Disputation weakens faith and so its merit.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e581.summary: Third objection: a work done purely for God is more meritorious than one mixed with a temporal motive, so faith mixed with human reason has less merit.
claims: Mixing reason with faith dilutes its purity of motive.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e584.summary: Sed contra: human reasons elucidate faith, and eternal life is promised to those who elucidate (Sirach 24:31), which would not be so if elucidation diminished merit.
claims: Elucidating faith by reason is rewarded, so it does not diminish merit.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e591.summary: Second sed contra: the closer a virtue is to its end, the more meritorious it is. The end of faith is understanding of truth, which human reasons bring closer. So reason increases faith's merit.
claims: Reason brings faith nearer its end of understanding and so increases merit.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e601.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 1: some matters of faith are above human reason simply, and these are essentially of faith; others are above the reason of some people but not of all. Faith was necessary for both. God has given humans an end above nature, full participation in his beatitude, and one who tends freely to an end must know it in order to direct the means. So humans needed a knowledge exceeding their natural knowledge, given by the grace of faith. As grace perfecting the affect presupposes nature, so faith presupposes natural knowledge that reason can prove (that God exists, is one, incorporeal, intelligent), and faith also inclines those who cannot reach these by reason to assent to them. Following Maimonides, this was necessary for five reasons: the height of the matter, remote from the senses by which our life is nourished; the intellect's inability to actualize itself without a teacher, who is not available to everyone; the many prerequisites of philosophical knowledge of God, which few can master; the natural dullness of some, who still need knowledge of God to direct their lives; and the occupation of people with the necessities of life.
claims: Faith is necessary because God has ordained humans to a supernatural end, which they must know in order to direct their free actions.
Faith presupposes natural knowledge of God, as grace presupposes nature, and also extends to these preambles for those who cannot demonstrate them.
Following Maimonides, faith in demonstrable truths is needed because of the difficulty of the matter, the lack of teachers, the many prerequisites, natural dullness, and the press of daily life.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e604.summary: Reply to the first objection: the end of human life is knowledge of God, even according to the philosophers, who place ultimate happiness in wisdom's contemplation of the noblest intelligible. Some knowledge of God, the vision by essence, exceeds our nature, and nature could not provide for that end, so faith in what essentially belongs to faith was necessary. Other knowledge of God is commensurate with our nature, by natural reason. But since this comes at the end of life, as its goal, while life must be ruled by knowledge of God from the start, nature could not sufficiently provide even for this. So what reason could not yet reach had to be known from the beginning by faith.
claims: Supernatural knowledge of God, the vision of his essence, cannot be provided by nature, so faith is required.
Even natural knowledge of God comes only at the end of inquiry, yet life must be governed by it from the start, so faith must supply it beforehand.
concepts: natural and supernatural knowledge of God

ta-l3d24q1-d1e607.summary: Reply to the second objection: the good is self-diffusive (Dionysius), so each mode of diffusion reveals a different ratio of goodness. Natural reason knows the highest good as communicating itself naturally, but not as communicating itself supernaturally, and it is under this latter ratio that the highest good is the end of our life. Faith is needed for it, since reason cannot reach it.
claims: The highest good as supernaturally self-communicating, which is our end, is known only by faith.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e610.summary: Reply to the third objection: the means must be proportioned to the end. Since the ultimate end exceeds nature and reason (which conjectures the end from the means), the means ordered to it must also exceed nature and reason. So not everything above reason in divine wisdom pertains to faith, only knowledge of the supernatural end and of the means by which we are supernaturally ordered to it.
claims: Faith covers knowledge of the supernatural end and the means to it, not everything in divine wisdom that exceeds reason.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e619.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 2: praise properly concerns a relation to something worthier (Ethics I). The concupiscible's act is praised as ordered to reason, reason's as ordered to the intellect that directs it, and the highest powers' acts as fittingly related to the end. That is why the best things are not praised but honoured. Virtue is the disposition of the perfect to the best, so its act is properly praiseworthy. Our natural knowledge stands to divine knowledge as lower to higher, so when our reason consents to the divine, its act is praiseworthy, as when the irascible submits to reason. Hence believing first truth in what is unseen is praiseworthy, meritorious and an act of virtue.
claims: Praise attaches to right order toward something higher.
Human reason's submission to divine truth is praiseworthy, as the passions' submission to reason is.
Believing first truth about what is unseen is praiseworthy, meritorious and virtuous.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e622.summary: Reply to the first objection: believing another human without a probable reason is believing too quickly, since one person's knowledge is not naturally ordered to be ruled by another's. But human knowledge is so ordered to first truth.
claims: Human knowledge is naturally ordered to be ruled by first truth, though not by another human's knowledge.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e625.summary: Reply to the second objection: in believing one does not renounce reason by acting against it but transcends it, relying on a higher director, first truth. Matters of faith are above reason, not against it. To seek what is above humanity is praiseworthy, since humans should raise themselves to divine things as far as they can (Aristotle).
claims: Faith transcends reason rather than contradicting it.
Striving toward divine things beyond human reach is praiseworthy.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e628.summary: Reply to the third objection: one has discernment of what is to be believed through the light of faith, as discernment of spirits through a charism. So one who has the light of faith does not consent to what is contrary to faith unless they abandon faith's inclination through their own fault.
claims: The light of faith supplies discernment in matters beyond reason.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e637.summary: Solution to quaestiuncula 3: the measure of merit can be considered from the work and from the worker. The work must be virtuous, and since virtue concerns the difficult and good, what adds difficulty or goodness to the work adds merit on the side of the work. On the worker's side the will is required, so the more willingly one acts, the more one merits, and merit's quantity always follows the root of charity. This second measure is quasi-formal and the surer guide to merit. Natural reason may be brought to bear for or against faith. Reasons against faith add difficulty, so with the same will to believe, one who believes despite seeing many contrary reasons merits more, as one who resists stronger temptation. Reasons for faith do not make the believed seen and so do not, of themselves, reduce the difficulty, but they make the will more ready to believe and so can increase merit, as a virtue makes a difficult act easy. So reasons both for and against faith, of themselves, increase merit, though either can diminish it through the believer's fault.
claims: Merit is measured by the difficulty and goodness of the work and, more formally, by the will and charity of the worker.
Contrary reasons increase merit by adding difficulty for one who still believes.
Supporting reasons increase merit by making the will readier to believe without making the object seen.
Either kind of reason can diminish merit only through the believer's fault.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e640.summary: Reply to the first objection: a reason that sufficiently proves the faith produces vision and so removes the difficulty of believing, but no such reason is available for what belongs to faith per se.
claims: No sufficient proof exists for articles of faith per se.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e643.summary: Reply to the second objection: faith is corrupted by disputations only in one who does not hold it firmly, through their own fault.
claims: Disputation harms faith only in the weak believer, by their fault.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e646.summary: Reply to the third objection: adducing human reason does not keep one from believing purely for God, since without the reason one would still believe. Of itself it diminishes merit only through the believer's fault.
claims: Reasons do not compromise the purity of faith's motive if one would believe without them.

ta-l3d24q1-d1e657.summary: Exposition of difficult phrases in Lombard's text. On 'which is not properly called faith but truth': faith is contrasted not with truth as such but with the manifest truth that succeeds it. On 'from faith in words': faith is not 'of words' as its object, which would make faith differ by language, but the things believed are proposed to us in words that show them insufficiently. On 'since faith is from hearing', and the objection that interior hearing does not differ from sight: both are said of the intellect by likeness, and the intellect has vision of things whose forms are presented to it and hearing of things it does not see. Some things we do not believe unless we understand them, such as naturally known principles, and some we do not understand unless we believe them, namely what is above reason; 'believe' here means any assent. 'Unless one understands something' means understanding what the name signifies.
claims: Faith is contrasted with the manifest truth of vision, not with truth as such.
Faith is not of words but of realities proposed insufficiently through words.
The intellect 'sees' what is presented by its form and 'hears' what it does not see.
Some truths must be understood to be believed and others believed to be understood.
concepts: vision and hearing of the intellect

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e126.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether uncreated truth is faith's object. The objections cite created content in the creed, Scripture and prophecy, the inertness of universals, and created beatitude. The sed contra cites Dionysius and the naming of faith as theological.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e154.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether faith concerns complex truths. The objections cite the simplicity of first truth, the incomplex object of vision and charity, and the problems of time and of changing tensed propositions. The sed contra places faith with science and opinion and notes that Christians and Jews differ over propositions.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e182.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether anything false can fall under faith. The objections cite contingent articles, God's power to redeem otherwise, the fallibility of hope and charity, and errors in worship. The sed contra cites faith's superior certainty and its character as a virtue.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e208.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. An object has formal, material and accidental elements, and the formal element specifies the power. First truth is the formal object of faith, as light is of sight, while what is believed about God (such as the passion) is material and what follows from it accidental. The replies treat created articles and scriptural narratives as material or accidental, distinguish faith from prophecy by formal aspect, and explain how first truth moves to action and relates to created beatitude.
claims: The formal object of faith is first truth; created matters are its material object.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e233.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. Since assent is to truth, which exists in composition, faith's object is propositional; 'I believe the incarnation' means 'I believe that it is or was'. Because we can know only that God is, not what he is, our knowledge of first truth is propositional. The replies explain the conceptual multiplicity of the simple God, the resolution of propositional knowledge into the vision of the incomplex, and the identity of faith across history: an article's time is accidental, so faith varies only in accident.
claims: Faith's object is a complex truth, and the articles remain essentially the same across time while their tense varies accidentally.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e258.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula: faith rests on infallible first truth, so nothing false can fall under it. Contingent events fall under faith as foreknown by God, with necessity of consequence. God's absolute power does not falsify faith. Hope and charity are not deceived, only human estimation. Error about whether a particular host is consecrated belongs to human judgment, not faith.
claims: Nothing false can fall under faith, because it rests on first truth and regards contingents as divinely foreknown.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e289.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether faith concerns what is seen. The objections cite Paul's 'seeing in a mirror', the analogy of the light of faith to natural light, understanding as seeing, prophecy, and the visibility of faith's material object. The sed contra cites Hebrews 11:1, John 1:18 and faith's link to hope.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e342.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether faith can concern what is known scientifically. The objections cite the demonstrability of God's existence, faith through teaching, reasons for faith (1 Peter 3:15, Richard of St Victor), and compelling miracles. The sed contra notes that science requires understood principles and that the matters of faith are above reason.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e381.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether the objects of faith are unknown. The objections cite Gregory on agnitio, 1 Corinthians 2:9, the origin of knowledge in sense, and the absence of faith's objects. The sed contra notes that faith is a cognitive habit and that unbelief is ignorance.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e423.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. 'Vision' applies loosely to all knowledge, and in that sense faith is an inner seeing. Properly it applies to knowledge in which the intelligible form is present by intellectual light, together with first principles, prophetic content and demonstrated conclusions. In this proper sense faith is not of things seen, since God eludes our intellect in this life and the articles cannot be demonstrated. The replies explain that the articles will be self-evident in the beatific vision, that belief requires only the meaning of terms, and that faith attains its material object only under its unseen formal ratio.
claims: Faith is not of things seen in the proper sense of vision.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e448.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. What exceeds all human understanding belongs to faith per se and cannot be known scientifically. Preambles such as God's existence can be demonstrated and are believed only per accidens by those who cannot follow the demonstration. Teaching that proposes without proving does not produce science. Faith stands to God's knowledge as a subalternate science to a higher one, human reason defends faith without proving it, and miracles prove the messenger's credibility, not the articles.
claims: The articles of faith per se cannot be scientifically known, though preambles to faith can be.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e470.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula. Perfect knowledge requires proposal, adherence and vision. The matters of faith are proposed through inadequate words and likenesses and adhered to without being seen, so they are known imperfectly, 'in a mirror and an enigma', but not wholly unknown. The replies explain agnitio, the sense of 'entering the heart', the sensory origin of faith in words, and faith's likeness to hearing about the absent.
claims: Objects of faith are known imperfectly, neither seen nor wholly unknown.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e501.summary: Arguments on the first quaestiuncula, whether it is necessary to believe what exceeds natural reason. The objections claim that providence made natural reason sufficient, that reason knows the highest good, and that we cannot know all that exceeds reason. The sed contra cites the higher life of grace and the supra-rational objects of hope.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e534.summary: Arguments on the second quaestiuncula, whether believing the unseen is praiseworthy. The objections cite credulity, the renunciation of reason, and the lack of discernment. The sed contra cites 'blessed are those who have not seen' and faith as a virtue.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e567.summary: Arguments on the third quaestiuncula, whether human reason diminishes the merit of faith. The objections cite Gregory's dictum, the corrosive effect of disputation, and the purity of motive. The sed contra cites the reward for elucidating faith and reason's bringing faith nearer its end, understanding.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e596.summary: Solution to the first quaestiuncula. Faith is necessary because humans are ordered to a supernatural end, which they must know in order to direct their free actions. Faith also covers the preambles reason can prove, because of the five obstacles Maimonides names (difficulty, lack of teachers, prerequisites, dullness, the press of life). The replies add that even natural knowledge of God comes too late to govern life without faith, that reason knows the highest good only in its natural self-communication, and that faith extends only to the supernatural end and its means.
claims: Faith is necessary for the supernatural end and, for most people, for the preambles reason could prove.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e614.summary: Solution to the second quaestiuncula. Praise attaches to right order toward something higher, so reason's assent to first truth is praiseworthy, meritorious and virtuous. Human knowledge is naturally ordered to be ruled by first truth, though not by another human. Faith transcends reason without contradicting it, and the light of faith provides discernment.
claims: Believing first truth about the unseen is praiseworthy and meritorious, being reason's right submission to a higher truth.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e632.summary: Solution to the third quaestiuncula. Merit is measured by the work's difficulty and goodness and, more formally, by the will and charity of the worker. Reasons against faith increase merit by adding difficulty, and reasons for faith increase it by making the will readier, though either can diminish it through the believer's fault. No sufficient proof of the articles exists, disputation harms only the weak, and reasons need not compromise faith's purity of motive.
claims: Human reason, for or against faith, of itself increases rather than diminishes the merit of faith.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e100.summary: Prooemium to Distinction 24. Lombard now treats faith in relation to its object, asking whether faith concerns the unseen and the unknown. The question's three articles are announced: the object of faith, its relation to our knowledge, and the merit and praise of faith.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e118.summary: Article 1 determines the object of faith. Using the analogy of light and colour, Aquinas distinguishes formal, material and accidental elements in the object. First truth, uncreated, is the formal object through which anything is credible; the created things believed about God (the passion, the incarnation) are material; their consequences are accidental. The object of faith is propositional, since assent is to truth and truth lies in composition, and since we know only that God is, not what he is. So the articles' tensed variation affects only an accidental element, and the faith of the patriarchs and of Christians is essentially the same. Nothing false can fall under faith, since it rests on infallible first truth and attains contingents as foreknown by God.
claims: First truth is the formal object of faith, and created matters are its material object.
The object of faith is a complex truth, whose temporal aspect is accidental, so faith is the same across history.
Nothing false can fall under faith, since it rests on first truth and attains contingents as foreknown by God.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e281.summary: Article 2 relates faith to human knowledge. Faith is not of things seen in the proper sense, since vision requires the intelligible form to be present by intellectual light or the matter to be resolvable into evident principles, and God eludes our intellect in this life. The articles will become self-evident only in the beatific vision. Faith cannot concern what is scientifically known per se. What exceeds all human understanding cannot be demonstrated, though preambles such as God's existence can be demonstrated and are believed only per accidens. Human reason can defend faith and miracles can attest the messenger, but neither proves the articles, which stand to God's knowledge as a subalternate science to its higher science. The objects of faith are nonetheless not wholly unknown: they are proposed in inadequate words and likenesses and adhered to without vision, and so known imperfectly.
claims: Faith is not of things seen, because neither God nor the articles are evident to us in this life.
What belongs to faith per se cannot be scientifically known, though the preambles of faith can be demonstrated.
The objects of faith are known imperfectly, through words and likenesses, with adherence but without vision.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e493.summary: Article 3 treats the necessity, praise and merit of faith. Faith is necessary because God has ordered humans to a supernatural end that they must know in order to pursue it freely. Faith also extends to preambles reason could prove, because of the obstacles Maimonides lists and because knowledge of God must guide life from its start. Believing first truth about what is unseen is praiseworthy and meritorious, since reason's submission to divine truth is right order to a higher rule, a transcending of reason rather than its contradiction, with the light of faith providing discernment. Human reasoning about faith, whether supportive or opposed, of itself increases merit, adding difficulty or readiness of will, and diminishes it only through the believer's fault.
claims: Faith is necessary because humans are ordered to a supernatural end and because natural knowledge of God is difficult and late.
Believing the unseen on divine authority is praiseworthy and meritorious, transcending reason without opposing it.
Rational arguments for or against faith increase its merit of themselves.

ta-l3d24q1-Dd1e652.summary: Exposition of Lombard's text. It clarifies that faith is contrasted with the manifest truth of vision, that faith is not of words but of realities proposed insufficiently in words, that the intellect 'sees' what is present through its form and 'hears' what it does not see, and that some truths must be understood in order to be believed and others believed in order to be understood.
claims: Faith concerns realities proposed through words, not the words themselves.

ta-l3d24q1.summary: The single question of Distinction 24 treats faith in relation to its object and to human knowledge. Article 1 identifies first truth as the formal object of faith, through which anything is credible, as light is to colour. Created realities such as the passion are its material object. The object is propositional, and the articles' tensed variation is accidental, so faith is the same in the patriarchs and in Christians. Nothing false can fall under faith, since it rests on infallible first truth and regards contingents as divinely foreknown. Article 2 shows that faith is neither of things seen nor of things scientifically known, since God and the articles are not evident to us in this life. Preambles such as God's existence are demonstrable and believed only per accidens, reason defends but does not prove the faith, and the objects of faith are known imperfectly 'in a mirror and an enigma'. Article 3 argues that faith is necessary because of humanity's supernatural end and the practical obstacles to natural knowledge of God. Believing the unseen on divine authority is praiseworthy and meritorious, and rational arguments for or against faith of themselves increase its merit. An expositio clarifies faith's relation to words, hearing and understanding. The question sets out how faith is a true but non-evident cognition of first truth, between ignorance and vision.
claims: The formal object of faith is first truth; its material object is what is believed about God, including created realities.
Faith concerns complex truths whose temporal aspect is accidental, so faith is one across history.
Faith is neither vision nor science of its per se objects, though preambles to faith can be demonstrated.
Faith is necessary for the supernatural end and is praiseworthy and meritorious, and reasoning about it can increase its merit.
